newsitem.title: FRANCE: France returns artwork to family robbed by Nazis.
newsitem.headline: France returns artwork to family robbed by Nazis.

text.p: France returned a valuable work of art on Wednesday to the heir of a Jewish family whose collection was stolen by the Nazis during World War Two.

At a ceremony in Paris, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette presented Antoinette Carvailho with "Les Glaneuses" (The Harvesters), a pastel drawing by Leon Augustin Lhermitte which was stolen from her father's chateau outside Paris in 1940.
"It is the state's role to watch out for the interests of the families who were robbed and to do justice," said de Charette.
"That is why I personally return to you this work by Lhermitte...It is proof of the government's desire to recover the stolen works and return them to their rightful owners."

The ceremony coincided with an investigation by Paris city authorities into the historic ownership of certain apartments in the capital following allegations some may have been seized from Jews fleeing persecution or deported to death camps.
Carvailho, heir to the Levi de Benzion family, said the Germans plundered about 950 artworks from her father's collection. Only a small number have been recovered.
"Right after the armistice, they came with a car... and they started taking everything away, and breaking everything," Carvailho told reporters.
The harvest scene, drawn in 1892, was one of 28 works stolen from various families by a German officer stationed in France during the war, according to the Foreign Ministry.
Towards the end of the war he asked a Wermacht soldier to take them back to Germany and keep them until his return.
But the officer never made it home and the soldier gave the works to a priest in Magdebourg, then in East Germany, during confession.
In 1972, the priest handed over the artworks to the Berlin State Museum, and after German reunification, France and Germany were able to trace some of the stolen works.

As soon as German Chancellor Helmut Kohl returned the paintings and drawings to France in 1994, they were exhibited at Paris's Musee d'Orsay in the hope they would be recognised by their rightful owners.

"I immediately recognised the drawing that had belonged to my parents," said Carvailho. She was able to prove ownership by finding an inventory of some of her father's paintings that included three works by Lhermitte.
Twenty of the works stolen by the German officer, including paintings and drawings by Claude Monet, Camille Pisarro, Eugene Delacroix and Edouard Manet, have yet to be claimed.
Seven others, including two by Jean-Baptiste Corot and one by Paul Gauguin, have been returned to their rightful owners, who preferred to keep their identities secret.
